teaser.text: GE Aerospace sells aircraft engines and equipment, then earns repeat revenue keeping them in service. Its business is easiest to understand as a long loop in which an engine sale creates decades of parts, repairs and technical support.

blocks.heading: Where could GE Aerospace's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted case puts GE at US$281.23 in October 2027, with the outcome hinging on profitable service growth and execution on supply, LEAP and CPP. By October 2029, the weighted price reaches US$323.37, a +7% return after a −8% return in October 2027, dividends included.
By October 2029, the modeled range is $174.46 to $508.79. Today’s price is $308.20. The bear case receives 25% probability, the base case 55%, and the bull case 20%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for GE Aerospace?

paragraphs.text: The bear story begins with supplier or shop constraints delaying deliveries and cash conversion. LEAP service costs then weaken margins, while CPP financing limits buybacks. The first price is $216.44 and the last is $174.46. Its 25% probability reflects the size of the pending acquisition, CES margin pressure and the absence of a guaranteed repurchase amount.

The bull story requires supplier flow to improve, CPP capacity to become productive and LEAP durability to reduce repair costs. Stronger service conversion would lift earnings and cash flow, supporting both buybacks and a premium P/E. The first price is $336.89 and the last is $508.79. Its 20% probability reflects the need for several operational improvements to arrive together.

blocks.heading: How much cash does GE Aerospace really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash reflects collections from customers and payments to suppliers, employees and others. Straightforward free cash flow subtracts capital spending from that operating cash. GE’s own measure makes additional adjustments, including separation-related cash costs and, from Q3 2025, proceeds from selling property and equipment.

blocks.heading: How much does GE Aerospace pay shareholders?

paragraphs.text: The dividend starts from the declared quarterly rate of $0.47, implying $1.88 through October 2027. The base case then rises to $2.00 and $2.12. The bear case holds at $1.88, while the bull case reaches $2.36. The range reflects 2026 free-cash-flow guidance of $8,900 million to $9,200 million, balanced against CPP funding and investment needs.

blocks.heading: Does GE Aerospace's dividend fit its cash flow?

paragraphs.text: The balance then shifted. In both 2024 and 2025, dividends and buybacks exceeded free cash flow. Buybacks reduce the number of shares outstanding, which can increase each remaining shareholder’s claim on earnings, but only if GE does not overpay. GE also issued shares through exercised employee options, so repurchases must be judged against both the price paid and new shares created.

blocks.heading: What could change GE Aerospace's dividend?

paragraphs.text: By October 2028, LEAP service margins and repair economics become decisive. Improving durability and expanding shop throughput would justify higher earnings, dividends and buybacks. Disappointing repair costs would reduce all three.

blocks.heading: What is GE Aerospace's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Dividends and buybacks return money to shareholders, but neither creates the underlying cash. Engine deliveries, flying activity, replacement parts and completed overhauls must support them. The stated real free cash flow yield therefore matters only once its adjustment is clearly defined.

earnings.closing: The full memo also explains GE Aerospace's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has GE Aerospace guided for 2026?

paragraphs.text: Management guides for 2026 operating profit of US$10,550–10,750 million and adjusted EPS of US$7.65–7.85. It guides to company free cash flow of US$8,900–9,200 million, with about half of the increase attributed to earnings and half to working capital.

blocks.heading: How have GE Aerospace revenue and profit changed?

paragraphs.text: Revenue, operating income, net income and diluted EPS all increased from the prior-year quarter. Commercial Engines & Services drove the expansion: its revenue grew 27%, with services up 26%. Equipment grew 30%.

The mix mattered. CES profit increased 20%, but its margin fell from 28.9% to 27.3%. GE attributed the pressure to installation-engine growth, including GE9X, as well as investment and inflation. A factory can therefore deliver more engines and earn more total profit while making less profit on each dollar of revenue. Those engines may still create a valuable service fleet later.

blocks.heading: What should GE Aerospace watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: The next evidence will show whether GE’s stronger output is becoming durable cash. The October 20, 2026 earnings report should show whether record shop production continued and whether new-engine deliveries still pressured margins. The January 21, 2027 full-year release should establish whether GE met its profit and cash outlook.
GE’s plan therefore depends on four things arriving together: more shop capacity, profitable service work, a workable CPP financing plan, and no major surprise from its legacy obligations.
